options: The pipeline's definition is a plain text file, versioned in the same repository it builds
The pipeline is configured entirely through a web UI with no file involved
Pipelines can only be written in Python
The pipeline runs only once and is then deleted
questions.explain: Pipeline as code means the definition itself is a committed, versioned file — reviewable and reproducible like any other code.

questions.q: In GitHub Actions vocabulary, what triggers a workflow to run?
options: An event, such as a push, a pull request, or a schedule
A runner
A step
A job
questions.explain: An event is what kicks off the workflow — everything else (runner, job, steps) happens as a result of that trigger.

questions.q: What is a 'job' in a GitHub Actions workflow?
options: A set of steps that run together on one runner
The machine that executes the work
A single command within a larger sequence
The event that triggers the workflow
questions.explain: A job groups an ordered list of steps together, all executed on the same runner.

questions.q: In the example workflow file, what does `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` specify?
options: The runner — the machine that executes the job
The event that triggers the workflow
The name of the repository
The dbt version to install
questions.explain: runs-on: selects which runner (machine/environment) the job executes on.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does pipeline as code beat configuring a pipeline through a UI?
options: It's reviewable as a diff, reproducible across every branch, and recoverable via git log and git revert
UI-based pipelines run faster in every case
It requires no testing at all
It eliminates the need for a repository
questions.explain: A file-based pipeline gets the same review, versioning, and rollback benefits as any other tracked code.
